Category: PSF 1: Enabling and continually improving effective efficient and convenient communications

Definition: Is there a structured onboarding and training program that focuses on empathy, company culture, and communication skills?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: No formal onboarding. New staff are expected to learn on the job by shadowing peers. Empathy and communication are assumed rather than taught.
Level 2 - Developing: Basic HR onboarding exists, but it is generic. There is a checklist of technical tasks, but no specific training module for soft skills.
Level 3 - Defined: A documented program specifically for Service Desk staff includes modules on active listening, empathy, and organizational culture. All new hires complete it.
Level 4 - Managed: The effectiveness of the training is measured via 30/60/90-day reviews. Post-training performance (e.g. first-month CSAT) is tracked to identify training gaps.
Level 5 - Optimized: Training is a living program. It is updated quarterly based on actual call recordings or chat transcripts to address real-world communication trends or challenges.

Definition: Do role profiles clearly define the competencies required for user interaction?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Job descriptions are non-existent or borrowed from generic IT templates. They focus almost entirely on technical skills (e.g. knows Windows 11).
Level 2 - Developing: Role profiles exist and mention good communication skills, but these are not defined as measurable competencies.
Level 3 - Defined: Every role (Agent, Lead, Manager) has a competency profile that explicitly lists soft skills like Conflict Resolution, Empathy, and Technical Translation.
Level 4 - Managed: These competencies are used as the primary scoring mechanism in annual performance reviews. Pay increases or promotions are tied to moving up the competency scale.
Level 5 - Optimized: Role profiles are dynamically adjusted based on the value stream. As automation takes over simple tasks, profiles are updated to prioritize high-level emotional intelligence and problem-solving.

Definition: Is there a formal program to monitor employee satisfaction (NPS/ESAT) and use it to drive improvements?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Employee satisfaction is not measured. Management only becomes aware of issues when someone resigns or an exit interview happens.
Level 2 - Developing: Informal pulse checks happen occasionally, or staff participate in a generic company-wide annual survey that lacks Service Desk specific context.
Level 3 - Defined: A Service Desk-specific ESAT (Employee Satisfaction) or eNPS (Employee Net Promoter Score) is conducted at least twice a year with high participation.
Level 4 - Managed: Data is analyzed to find root causes of burnout or dissatisfaction. Results are shared transparently with the team, and an action plan is created.
Level 5 - Optimized: Employee Experience (EX) is treated as a lead indicator for User Experience (UX). Management can demonstrate a direct correlation between improved staff satisfaction and higher customer CSAT.

Definition: Are omnichannel capabilities (AI, Chatbots, Voice Assistants) implemented and aligned with user preferences?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Users can use phone or email, but the data is separate. No AI or bots. A user has to repeat their story if they switch channels.
Level 2 - Developing: Phone, email, and maybe a basic web-chat feed into one tool. The desk knows a user's history across channels, but interaction is still 100% human-led.
Level 3 - Defined: A chatbot or portal is the primary entry point. Users can switch between channels (e.g. start on Chat, move to Phone) seamlessly. Channel choice is based on user feedback/data.
Level 4 - Managed: Chatbots use Natural Language Processing (NLP) to resolve common requests. The organization tracks Channel Migration and ensures the digital experience is preferred over the manual one.
Level 5 - Optimized: The system offers the best channel based on the specific issue (e.g. this looks complex; would you like a call back?). Voice assistants are integrated for hands-free support.

Definition: Is AI-driven sentiment analysis used to evaluate and improve the quality of user interactions?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Interaction quality is only reviewed if a user complains formally or a manager happens to listen to a random call.
Level 2 - Developing: Managers manually audit a small percentage of tickets or calls (e.g. 5 per agent per month) to judge tone and helpfulness.
Level 3 - Defined: The ITSM tool automatically flags tickets as Positive, Neutral, or Negative based on keywords. This data is used in monthly performance reports.
Level 4 - Managed: Sentiment analysis runs in real-time. If a chat or call turns Negative, a supervisor is alerted to intervene. Analysis is used to identify specific staff training needs.
Level 5 - Optimized: The system analyzes historical data to predict if a user is likely to be frustrated (e.g. after 2 failed password resets) and proactively routes them to a high-empathy agent.

Definition: Is a Knowledge Base actively maintained and accessible for user self-service?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Knowledge is in people's heads or buried in old PDFs/Word docs on a shared drive. Users have no way to help themselves.
Level 2 - Developing: A Knowledge Base exists within the ITSM tool, but it is only for Service Desk agents. Users must still contact the desk to get the information.
Level 3 - Defined: A user-facing portal provides How-To articles. Content is reviewed on a schedule. Search functionality allows users to find basic solutions.
Level 4 - Managed: Article creation is part of the ticket resolution process. The organization measures Knowledge Deflection (how many tickets were NOT opened because of the KB).
Level 5 - Optimized: Knowledge is pushed to the user based on context (e.g. if a user opens a specific app, the top 3 tips appear). AI summarizes long articles into quick answers.

Definition: Are vendor-managed support functions integrated into the communication flow to ensure a seamless user experience?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Users are given a separate phone number or email for the vendor. The internal Service Desk has no visibility into the status of vendor-held tickets.
Level 2 - Developing: The Service Desk logs a ticket and then manually contacts the vendor. Updates are manually copied back and forth between systems.
Level 3 - Defined: Basic Ticket Bonding (e-bonding) is in place. When the Service Desk assigns a ticket to a vendor, it appears in the vendor's system, and status changes sync back.
Level 4 - Managed: The user can see vendor updates in real-time via the internal portal. The Service Desk measures Vendor Responsiveness as part of the end-to-end communication metric.
Level 5 - Optimized: The vendor acts as a seamless extension of the desk. AI-driven routing sends tickets to the right partner automatically, and the user experience is identical regardless of who solves it.

Definition: Do third-party providers adhere to the same communication standards as internal staff?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Vendors use their own templates, branding, and tone of voice. Users often get confused about who they are talking to.
Level 2 - Developing: Vendors are asked to include the company name in their emails (e.g. Support on behalf of Company X), but the quality and tone remain inconsistent.
Level 3 - Defined: Communication standards (tone, response times, language requirements) are written into the Underpinning Contracts (UC) or SOWs.
Level 4 - Managed: Vendor communications are audited using the same criteria as internal staff. CSAT scores are broken down by Internal vs. Partner to ensure parity.
Level 5 - Optimized: Vendor staff attend the same Service Empathy and Company Culture workshops as internal employees. They are treated as one unified support community.

Definition: Are standardized communication channels established, and is user awareness of these channels measured?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Users find help through word-of-mouth or by calling individual technicians directly. There is no official list of supported channels.
Level 2 - Developing: A list of channels (Phone, Email, Portal) exists in the Service Catalog, but user awareness is low, and shadow support (users bypassing the desk) is common.
Level 3 - Defined: A formal Communication Plan is in place. Channels are branded and marketed to the business. Users know exactly where to go for what type of issue.
Level 4 - Managed: The organization measures Channel Stickiness and awareness levels. Promotion campaigns are run to move users from expensive channels (phone) to convenient ones (portal).
Level 5 - Optimized: The organization uses in-app prompts and contextual marketing to guide users to the most efficient channel based on their current activity or location.

Definition: Are there defined response and resolution times for user interactions?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: There are no formal targets for when a user should receive an initial response or a final resolution. Tickets stay open indefinitely.
Level 2 - Developing: The Service Desk has internal goals for response times, but these are not shared with or agreed upon by the business.
Level 3 - Defined: Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for different priority levels are documented, agreed with customers, and visible to users when they log a ticket.
Level 4 - Managed: The focus shifts from SLA compliance to Experience Level Agreements. The desk measures Wait Time Satisfaction rather than just Time to Answer.
Level 5 - Optimized: The system provides real-time Estimated Time to Resolve to the user based on current queue volumes and technician availability, managing expectations perfectly.

Definition: Is user feedback (CSAT) directly integrated into the continual improvement initiatives for the desk?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: The only feedback received is through unsolicited complaints or praise. No structured survey mechanism exists.
Level 2 - Developing: Transactional surveys (CSAT) are sent after a ticket closes. Results are filed away but rarely lead to specific process changes.
Level 3 - Defined: CSAT data is reviewed in monthly management meetings. Bad scores trigger a standard follow-up process with the user to understand the issue.
Level 4 - Managed: Feedback trends directly populate the CSI Register. For example, if users complain about slow chat, a formal improvement project is launched and tracked.
Level 5 - Optimized: The organization can demonstrate multiple instances where a user suggestion led to a significant redesign of a service or communication workflow.

Category: PSF 2: Enabling the effective integration of user communications into value streams

Definition: Does leadership effectively position the Service Desk as a valued business partner across the organization?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Leadership views the Service Desk as a cost center or a necessary evil. The desk is not mentioned in company-wide communications or town halls.
Level 2 - Developing: IT leadership acknowledges the desk's importance for keeping the lights on, but business stakeholders still view it as a technical hurdle rather than a partner.
Level 3 - Defined: The Service Desk is formally introduced to new business units. Leadership ensures the desk is consulted during the Design and Transition of new business services.
Level 4 - Managed: IT leadership promotes the desk by showcasing how support efficiency has protected business revenue or productivity. The desk has a seat at the table in service review meetings.
Level 5 - Optimized: The Service Desk is recognized as a Business Intelligence Hub. Leadership uses insights from the desk to influence corporate strategy and digital transformation.

Definition: Do staff understand the direct link between their support activities and specific business outcomes?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Staff focus solely on closing tickets. They do not know what the business units do or how a specific system failure impacts the company's bottom line.
Level 2 - Developing: Staff know which department a user belongs to and have a general sense of High Priority apps, but they lack specific context on business cycles (e.g. end-of-quarter rush).
Level 3 - Defined: Agents are trained on the Business Impact of the services they support. They can explain why a specific request is critical to a business outcome (e.g. this affects payroll processing).
Level 4 - Managed: Performance metrics are tied to business uptime. Staff can see how their First Contact Resolution (FCR) directly correlates to saved business man-hours.
Level 5 - Optimized: Staff proactively suggest changes to value streams because they see where business processes are failing. They act as Business Advocates within the IT department.

Definition: Is there a fair remuneration package aligned with productivity and development goals?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Pay is based on tenure alone. There are no incentives for performance or skill acquisition, leading to a minimum effort culture and high turnover.
Level 2 - Developing: A standard bonus structure exists (e.g. if the company does well, you get 2%), but it isn't linked to individual Service Desk performance or professional growth.
Level 3 - Defined: Remuneration tiers are clearly defined and linked to a Competency Matrix. Staff get raises for completing certifications (e.g. ITIL, Technical certs) or mastering new roles.
Level 4 - Managed: A portion of the package is at risk and tied to high-value metrics like NPS (Net Promoter Score), Team Productivity, and Quality of Value Stream integration.
Level 5 - Optimized: The package includes development sabbaticals, intrapreneurship bonuses for innovation, and long-term incentives that make the Service Desk a career destination, not a stepping stone.

Definition: Does the toolset support automation for ticket categorization and routing to optimize the value stream?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Manual Triage - Every ticket is read by a human dispatcher who manually selects the category and assigns it to a team. This creates a massive bottleneck.
Level 2 - Developing: Rule-based Routing - The tool uses basic If/Then logic (e.g. if the user selects Hardware, route to the Desktop Team). Categorization is still prone to human error.
Level 3 - Defined: Standardized Integration - The tool automatically categorizes and routes tickets based on keywords, user profile data, and service impact. Triage time is significantly reduced.
Level 4 - Managed: Machine Learning (ML) Categorization - The system learns from historical data to suggest categories and teams. The organization measures Routing Accuracy and Triage Velocity.
Level 5 - Optimized: Zero-touch Routing - AI autonomously routes tickets to the correct value stream with >95% accuracy. It can trigger automated workflows (e.g. Auto-provisioning) without human intervention.

Definition: Are predictive analytics used to anticipate user needs and prevent bottlenecks?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Reactive. The organization only looks at what happened yesterday. There is no attempt to look forward or predict spikes in volume.
Level 2 - Developing: Basic Trending. Management uses historical reports to guess when they might be busy (e.g. we are always busy on Mondays). No formal analytical models are used.
Level 3 - Defined: Trend Forecasting. The tool generates forecasts based on historical seasonality and upcoming changes (e.g. predicting a 20% spike during a major software rollout).
Level 4 - Managed: Early Warning Systems. Analytics identify clusters of incidents in real-time before they become major outages. The system alerts managers to potential queue bottlenecks before they happen.
Level 5 - Optimized: Proactive Prevention. Predictive models trigger proactive communications to users (e.g. we notice your disk space is low; click here to clean it) to prevent a ticket from ever being created.

Definition: Is there a remote support tool strategy that enables rapid diagnosis and resolution?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Ad-hoc. Agents use whatever free tool they can find, or they rely on over-the-shoulder verbal instructions to the user. No central security or logging.
Level 2 - Developing: Basic Screen Sharing. A standard tool (like Teams or Zoom) is used to see the user's screen, but agents lack administrative control or advanced diagnostic capabilities.
Level 3 - Defined: Integrated Remote Control. A dedicated tool (e.g. BeyondTrust, TeamViewer, LogMeIn) is integrated into the ITSM ticket. It allows file transfer, registry editing, and administrative bypass.
Level 4 - Managed: Unattended & Mobile Support. The strategy includes the ability to support mobile devices and unattended servers/workstations. Usage and Time-to-Resolve via Remote are tracked.
Level 5 - Optimized: Advanced Diagnostics/AR. The tool automatically pulls system logs and diagnostic data the moment the session starts. For physical issues, Augmented Reality (AR) is used to guide users.

Definition: Are there collaboration frameworks and ticket-bonding with third parties for seamless escalations?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Escalations happen via phone or generic support emails. There is no shared visibility; the Service Desk has to call the vendor just to get a status update.
Level 2 - Developing: The Service Desk has logins to the vendor's portal. This is stuttering integration - agents have to jump between tools and manually copy-paste data to keep internal tickets updated.
Level 3 - Defined: Systems are integrated (via API or middleware). A ticket assigned to a vendor bonds to their system. Status changes, comments, and attachments sync automatically.
Level 4 - Managed: Real-time dashboards show the health of the partner-integrated value stream. The organization measures Integration Latency and Vendor Triage Time automatically.
Level 5 - Optimized: The organization and partners share ChatOps environments (e.g. shared Slack/Teams channels with bot integration). AI monitors the joint flow and flags potential OLA breaches before they happen.

Definition: Is the impact of legacy systems support managed and optimized through partner agreements?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Legacy systems are supported on a best-effort basis. Knowledge often resides with a single person (internal or external) with no formal support contract.
Level 2 - Developing: An inventory of legacy systems exists. There is a keep-it-running agreement with a vendor, but no specific SLAs for these dinosaur systems.
Level 3 - Defined: Specific Legacy Care contracts are in place with defined SLAs. These agreements include Extended Support clauses and clear end-of-life (EOL) or migration dates.
Level 4 - Managed: The organization tracks the Total Cost of Legacy (including the friction it causes in modern value streams). Partners are incentivized to keep legacy systems stable while preparing for decommission.
Level 5 - Optimized: The partner takes full ownership of the legacy stack, providing modern wrappers (APIs) so these old systems can participate in new automated value streams without slowing them down.

Definition: Is the Service Desk involved in strategic IT initiatives and given notice of new support requirements?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: The Service Desk finds out about a new product or system when the first user calls to report it. There is zero involvement in project lifecycles.
Level 2 - Developing: The desk is notified a few days before Go-Live. They receive a basic document but have no time to train or provide input on supportability.
Level 3 - Defined: The Service Desk is a stakeholder in the Service Transition process. They attend CAB (Change Advisory Board) meetings and must sign off on support requirements before a project goes live.
Level 4 - Managed: The desk is involved during the Design phase. They provide data on past failures to ensure new services are supportable by design, reducing future incident volumes.
Level 5 - Optimized: The Service Desk helps define the IT roadmap. Leadership uses Service Desk pain points to decide which legacy systems to retire and which new technologies to invest in.

Definition: Are Business Outcomes (not just SLAs) incorporated into metrics (e.g. Total Cost of Incidents, Business Productivity)?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: The desk only tracks how many tickets they closed. No one knows if these tickets were important or how long the business was actually down.
Level 2 - Developing: Success is defined by Time to Resolve. While better, this doesn't capture the business impact (e.g. a 4-hour fix for 1 person vs. 1000 people is treated the same).
Level 3 - Defined: Incidents are categorized by business criticality. Reports start to highlight Business Hours Lost for key services.
Level 4 - Managed: The organization calculates the Total Cost of Incidents (TCOI) combining IT labor costs and lost business productivity. Reports speak in dollars lost rather than tickets closed.
Level 5 - Optimized: The Service Desk demonstrates Business Value Added. For example: by automating password resets, we returned 400 hours of productivity to the Sales team, worth $50,000 this month.

Definition: Has a workload mix study been conducted to align staffing levels with value stream demand?
Level 1 - Ad Hoc: Hiring is done when the team feels busy or when turnover gets too high. No data is used to justify headcounts.
Level 2 - Developing: Staffing is based on the average number of tickets per month. It doesn't account for the complexity of the work or the peaks and valleys of the business day.
Level 3 - Defined: A formal study (using tools like Erlang-C) accounts for arrival rates, handle times, and ticket complexity to ensure the right skills are available at the right times.
Level 4 - Managed: Staffing levels are adjusted based on the Value Stream (e.g. more staff on payroll day, fewer on training days). The organization tracks Utilization vs. Burnout rates.
Level 5 - Optimized: AI predicts workload spikes based on project calendars and historical patterns, automatically suggesting shift changes or gig-resource scaling before the rush hits.
